messages.subject_clean: estimating detection curve in non-discrete vegetation
messages.body_plain:
I have been surveying kangaroos via tracks, within open woodland and wood=
land vegetation types. It is not possible to assign entire transect to ea=
ch vegetation type and yet density and visibility varies greatly between =
the vegetation types.=20=20
So for example, there are cases where a kangaroo is spotted in woodland v=
egetation at 70m, but for 50m of the 70m perpendicular distance, open woo=
dland occurs.=20=20
I thought about dividing line length based on extent of each vegetation t=
ype, then assigning species recorded in each vegetation type to a line. S=
o if kangaroo =E2=80=98A=E2=80=99 was seen in woodland, and woodland make=
s up 40% of vegetation, then 40% of line length is classified as woodland=
 stratum ,with the kangaroo =E2=80=98A=E2=80=99 observation included. How=
ever where kangaroo =E2=80=98A=E2=80=99 is seen in woodland, despite majo=
rity of distance from line being open woodland as in the above example, d=
etection probably is being miss-assigned.
I thought about assigning animals to different stratum based on the major=
ity of vegetation found from the line to the animal, not necessary where =
the animal occurred. So in above example the animal would be classed as b=
eing in open woodland, as majority of perpendicular line was in open wood=
land.=20
This problem must have occurred before, but I was unable to find a soluti=
on in the literature. Anyway help would be greatly appreciated.=20

messages.subject: Re: estimating detection curve in non-discrete vegetation
messages.subject_clean: estimating detection curve in non-discrete vegetation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brett, list,

You do not mention if you need, or not, density for each habitat (say=20
woodland vegetation WV and open woodland OW) or just a single density=20
estimate.

If the latter, then you could just have a single line transects, include=20
habitat as a covariate given it affects detection, and proceed.

If you do need density in each habitat, I wonder if the following=20
procedure might be useful. Consider conceptually two separate surveys.=20
For each survey, include only the distances made to animals in one of=20
the habitats. Lets consider WV here. Then, you have the wrong WV density=20
estimate (you are underestimating the density in that habitat, because=20
in reality the line length is way too big), but if you multiply that=20
density estimate by the total area, you should get the abundance=20
estimate for the WV area alone. Hence if you divide this by the area of=20
the WV habitat only, you get the density estimate in WV. You then to the=20
same for the OW, and you get the two separate density estimates.

This only makes sense if line placement was random with respect to=20
habitat to begin with, and that you have sufficient lines such that the=20
distribution of available animals with respect to the lines considering=20
each habitat separately can be assumed uniform.

Other might have additional suggestions, or might even want to tell us=20
that my suggestion sucks!

Cheers

T.

messages.subject: Re: estimating detection curve in non-discrete vegetation
messages.subject_clean: estimating detection curve in non-discrete vegetation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tiago,

I like the suggestion! However two things. While I have tried to ensure t=
racks were unbiased to vegetation types (used ArcGis to choose unbiased s=
urvey tracks) it would be nice not to have to assume this, as at some sit=
es no amount of cutting and adding can get tracks to unbiasedly sample ve=
getation.

Is there a reason why your suggestion is preferable to this option:

I estimate strip width (truncation distance) apply a buffer around my tra=
nsects (in ArcGis) then estimate vegetation proportion within that buffer=
. So, if line 1 (100m in length) with a 100m buffer, results in 70% open =
woodland and 30% woodland vegetation cover, I create two lines, one lengt=
h 70m, the other length 30m. Observation made along original lines are th=
en separated based on the vegetation type the animal was observed.

 To make sure I=E2=80=99m on the same page, in your option, if I have 20 =
transects, most of which cover different vegetation types I would make tw=
o versions of every transect where multiple vegetation types occur, then =
use a global estimate of vegetation area to separate into different strat=
um. So your option focuses on a global stratum, whereas the option I prov=
ided uses a transect level. Of course, the transects would also have to b=
e included under the woodland or open woodland stratum ultimately.

Your option seems easier, but does of course depend on unbiased sampling.=
 My option should account for this, where one vegetation type is over sam=
pled.

What do you think. I'm sure my option has problems, but I am yet to reali=
se them.

Brett

messages.subject: comparing multiple densities, z-tests or anova?
messages.subject_clean: comparing multiple densities, z-tests or anova?
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,
I am using point count distance sampling to estimate population density of parrots on an island. I have 268 points on a regular grid. I only visited every point once and have 0-4 detections per point. Although the total population estimate was the main focus I would also like to compare the parrot population density estimates between 5 habitat types (with unequal sample sizes).  I used separate detection functions for three of the habitats but had to use a common one for two scrub habitat types because the sample size in one of them was too small. I am prepared to exclude this habitat from my comparison if necessary, so I could have independent detection functions for my four habitat types.

I read the chapter on Estimating change in density in Introduction to Distance Sampling but that only explains how to compare two densities. I searched the archive and found several discussions on whether it is possible to use anovas for distance data. The answer seems to be yes, but how can I run an anova on the 5 density estimates specific to the habitats? I think I would need replicate density estimates, which I do not have.

If I wanted to use ANOVA, would I have to use point specific encounter rates? Using encounter rates seems to give up a lot of information, is this the best option?

Or can I do the comparisons pair by pair with z-tests and adjust the p-values for multiple comparisons? Or is there a method of multiple comparisons which I can use with the distance output for my habitat types?

Any help would be much appreciated
Anna Reuleaux

messages.body_plain:
Dear Catarina, list

I must start by telling you that regarding data entry, you should=20
probably read first the "Data Import" section on Distance 6 help files.=20
That will probably help you regarding some of the data import issues you=20
are mentioning.

Regarding some of the other issues you mention, here are some comments:

> > My case is the following: Rabbit census on an island, performed during =
2
> > nights each month from July 2006 to June 2009, along fixed linear trans=
ects
> > (n=3D7) in which a single observer would count number of rabbits seen
> > according to 5 classes of distance: 0 meters (road) and then 0-25m, 25-=
50m,
> > 50-75m and 75-100m.

The fact that you have a class just for distance 0, and further that you=20
say that corresponds to detections on the road, makes me wonder if data=20
import is not the least of your worries, because:

1. distance sampling from roads might be severely biased if the rabbits=20
distribution is not independent from the roads. The problem lies in the=20
fact that conventional methods require that the distribution of=20
available animals (detected or not) with respect to the transect lines=20
is uniform, something that is reasonable given a sufficient number of=20
randomly placed transect lines. If animals react to roads, and transects=20
are along roads, that is almost certainly not the case. Bias might be=20
severe, e.g. more than 100% by ignoring the road effect, see Marques et=20
al 2010 for an example with hares. You better than anyone will know if=20
this is an issue for your case study.

2. A class for distance 0 makes no sense from a distance sampling=20
perspective. The fact that you need one makes me wonder if you have a=20
very spiked detection. In the best case scenario you will end up using=20
only 4 distance classes (0-25),...,(75-100), but if you have lots of=20
detections 0, I wonder if there's more to it that it meets the eye.

> > My goal is to obtain density estimates for each month. Therefore, I
> > structured the .txt file with the following data: 1st column was date (=
1,2,3
> > according to the number of replica), transect_id, transect length, tota=
l

ld

This is not correct. Assuming all else was OK, you could have each month=20
as a stratum, and then get estimates by stratum, eventually pooling the=20
data from all strata for the detection function (depending on you sample=20
size in each month). But other data configurations might be possible. It=20
all depends on your specific objectives when implementing the analysis.

Hope this helps to some extent.

Feel free to contact me off the list for further questions if you think=20
I might be of assistance. And finally, welcome to the field, it's not=20
that often that other Portuguese people post here.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Several are available as example projects in Distance (see the last page of
Chapter 3 of the online help) and can easily be exported to other software.

The mrds analysis engine in Distance is actually an R library (see Chapter 10 of
the online help, under "Running the MRDS Analysis Engine from Outside Distance);
it can analyze single platform as well as double platform data (although at
present it only does key functions for detection functions and not adjustment
terms).  So, this might make a nice way to check your own R code.

Cheers, - Len
